Are small data methods still needed in the big data age? Why, and how?

Big data does not eliminate the need for systematic small data methodologies. In fact, it could be argued that it increases the need for the need for these methodologies. It is very important to understand the data generating process, as well as the context, representativeness, etc. of the sample itself. More is not better, just more. Without understanding these processes, the inference from the sample set is limited.

title: Assignment 02
text:
What you will produce: The same Google Trends series pulled two ways — once by hand from the website, once from R with gtrendsR — and a short note on what differs between them and why.

Collect the data from the Google Trends website


Go to https://trends.google.com and search Trump, Kamala Harris and Election.
Download the data as [csv](https://jmglendenning.github.io/(https://jmglendenning.github.io/time_series_US_20210912-0854_20260912-0854.csv)
Record the query

Query parameters

Search terms: Trump, Kamala Harris, Election
Geography: United States
Time window: Last five years
Category: All categories
Search type: Web Search
Date/time pulled: 2026-09-12T08:52:23-05:00
Additional current-news term: data center, United States,

Repeat the download using a current-news term of your choice: data center. Query parameters

Search terms: data center
Geography: United States
Time window: Last five years
Category: All categories
Search type: Web Search
Date/time pulled: 2026-09-12T08:52:23-05:00
Additional current-news term: data center, United States,


Look at what you got


Date range: [enter range]
Interval: [hourly / daily / weekly / monthly]
After changing the date window, the interval [did / did not] change. [brief explanation]
Google Trends values are normalized rather than raw search counts. A value of 100 represents the peak relative search interest within the query, while 0 indicates insufficient or very low relative interest.
After removing one search term, the remaining values [did / did not] stay the same. [brief explanation]


Collect the same data with gtrendsR


library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)

TrumpHarrisElection <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

the_df <- TrumpHarrisElection$interest_over_time
plot(TrumpHarrisElection)







# Cache the raw pull because later calls may return slightly different values.
write_csv(
  the_df,
  paste0("gtrends_us_5y_", Sys.Date(), ".csv")
)


One term over its full history:


tg <- gtrends("tariff", time = "all")
plot(tg)









The same term in another country:


plot(gtrends("tariff", geo = "GB", time = "all"))









One term across the United States, Great Britain, and Taiwan:


plot(gtrends("tariff", geo = c("US", "GB", "TW"), time = "all"))









Three terms worldwide:


tct <- gtrends(c("tariff", "China military", "Taiwan"), time = "all")
plot(tct)









With onlyInterest left at its default, names(tct) returns:


names(tct)

[1] "interest_over_time"  "interest_by_country" "interest_by_region" 
[4] "interest_by_dma"     "interest_by_city"    "related_topics"     
[7] "related_queries"    



The additional data frames that the website CSV did not provide were: [enter names and briefly describe them].


Search term versus intended concept


harris_compare <- gtrends(
  c("Harris", "Kamala Harris"),
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0,
  onlyInterest = TRUE
)

plot(harris_compare)









The Harris and Kamala Harris series [are / are not] the same. [describe the difference]
This difference shows that a search term is not necessarily identical to the concept being measured. Harris can refer to many people, places, or organizations, while Kamala Harris is a more specific query.


Compare the website and R methods


The website and gtrendsR series [were / were not] identical. The differences were [describe magnitude and direction].
Reproducibility: [compare whether another person could regenerate the same result]
Provenance: [compare how each method records query parameters]
Scale: [compare the practicality of collecting three terms versus many terms]
Fragility: [describe what can break and how failures would be detected]


Repeatability of the Google Trends sample

Run the same call twice a few minutes apart and compare the results.

pull_1 <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)$interest_over_time

# Run the second pull a few minutes later.
pull_2 <- gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)$interest_over_time


The two pulls [did / did not] return exactly the same values. [briefly quantify the difference]
Because Google Trends is based on a sample of searches, repeated pulls can vary. This means findings should be interpreted as estimates from a sampled and normalized source, and successful pulls should be cached for reproducibility.

Coin Hoard Data Generating Process
The data-generating process for coin hoards is inherently selective: hoards enter the archaeological record when people deliberately conceal coins and subsequently fail to recover them, while the observed dataset is further shaped by differential preservation, discovery, reporting, and publication.

Getting familiar with data import in R.

What are the most commonly used packages for importing data in R?


readr — delimited text files such as CSV
readxl — Excel files
haven — SPSS, Stata, and SAS files
jsonlite — JSON
xml2 — XML
arrow — Parquet, Feather, and Arrow IPC

For geospatial data, some of the common packages are:

sf — vector geospatial data such as Shapefile, GeoPackage, and GeoJSON
terra — raster geospatial data such as GeoTIFF and other GDAL-supported formats
stars — multidimensional raster and spatiotemporal data
lidR — LiDAR point-cloud data such as LAS and LAZ
rnaturalearth — Natural Earth country, boundary, coastline, and physical geography
gdalcubes — access and process large collections of Earth observation imagery
osmdata — OpenStreetMap data through the Overpass API
tigris — U.S. Census TIGER/Line geographic data


Conventional formats — CSV, SPSS, Stata, XML, JSON. Be able to name what reads each one.





Format
Common R package/function




CSV
readr::read_csv()


SPSS
haven::read_sav()


Stata
haven::read_dta()


XML
xml2::read_xml()


JSON
jsonlite::fromJSON()




New formats — Feather, Parquet, Arrow IPC, ORC, HDF5, Zarr, Avro. What problem does each one solve that CSV does not?








Format
Main advantage over CSV




Feather
Fast, typed, columnar exchange between data-analysis systems


Parquet
Compressed columnar storage optimized for large analytical datasets


Arrow IPC
Fast in-memory or interprocess exchange without repeated serialization


ORC
Compressed columnar storage designed for large-scale analytical workloads


HDF5
Efficient storage of large, complex, multidimensional scientific data


Zarr
Chunked, compressed multidimensional arrays suited to cloud/object storage


Avro
Schema-based row-oriented serialization useful for data exchange and streaming



New data formats exist because CSV is simple and portable but does not preserve data types, efficiently compress large datasets, support fast columnar access, or handle complex and multidimensional data well. This is especially problematic with geospatial data.
Bring the activated Census API key and the one-sentence explanation of why the new formats exist; class begins by pulling Census data live.
